questions.question: Explain why paper can be recycled, describe the stages of turning waste paper into new board, and state why fresh fibre must always be added.
questions.expected_answer: Paper is a mat of cellulose fibres bonded only by tangling and drying, not melted together, so water and agitation separate the fibres for reuse. Stages: collection from homes, shops and offices, largely by waste pickers and collection companies; sorting into grades and baling; pulping in a vat of water into a fibre slurry; screening and spinning to remove staples, tape and plastic, with de-inking by chemicals and air bubbles for white paper; spreading the pulp on a moving wire mesh to drain, pressing between rollers and drying on heated cylinders into a continuous sheet; layering, and gluing a fluted sheet between two liners for corrugated board. Each cycle shortens and weakens the fibres, and after about five to seven cycles they are too short, so fresh fibre from plantation timber or bagasse is blended in to keep board strong.

questions.question: Name four packaging products made from recycled paper, explain how moulded pulp products are formed, and describe how corrugated board uses a structural principle from Term 1.
questions.expected_answer: Corrugated shipping boxes (the largest product), moulded pulp egg trays, fruit trays, cup carriers and protective inserts, folding cartons for cereal and medicines with a thin white printing layer, paper bags, toilet-roll and tape cores and notepad backing board. Moulded pulp is formed by sucking pulp from low-grade waste paper onto a shaped mesh mould and drying it. Corrugated board works like an I-beam: two flat liners act as flanges in compression and tension while the fluted middle layer acts as the web holding them apart and carrying shear, so the board is far stiffer than a flat sheet of the same weight; egg trays use the shell shape of each cup to resist crushing.

questions.question: Evaluate paper recycling by listing its benefits and its limits, and give two recommendations for improving the system.
questions.expected_answer: Benefits: each tonne saves roughly 17 trees of plantation timber, about 26 000 litres of water and 60 to 70 percent of the energy of making paper from fresh pulp; keeps about three cubic metres out of landfill where paper would release methane; supports tens of thousands of jobs including 60 000 to 90 000 waste pickers; reduces pressure for new plantations. Limits: fibres wear out after five to seven cycles so fresh fibre is always needed; contamination by greasy, waxed, laminated or wet paper spoils bales; de-inking produces sludge; collection depends on sorting at source and on waste pickers working in poor conditions; recycled board is greyer and weaker so unsuitable for some uses; transport uses fuel. Recommendations: separate paper cleanly at home and school; design packaging for recycling by avoiding wax, laminates and solvent inks; formally recognise and pay waste pickers fairly to improve collection.
